segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He also said to the disciples,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “There was a rich man who had a manager, and charges were brought to him that this man was squandering his property.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So he called him and said, ‘What is this I hear about you? Give an account of your management, for you can no longer be manager.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The manager said to himself, ‘What shall I do, since my master is taking the management away from me? I am not strong enough to dig; I am ashamed to beg.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: I know what I will do, so that when I am removed from the management people will welcome me into their homes.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So he summoned his master’s debtors one by one. He said to the first, ‘How much do you owe my master?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said, ‘A hundred baths of olive oil.’ He told him, ‘Take your bill, sit down quickly, and write fifty.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then he said to another, ‘And you, how much do you owe?’ He said, ‘A hundred cors of wheat.’ He told him, ‘Take your bill and write eighty.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And the master praised the dishonest manager because he had acted shrewdly. For the children of this age are shrewder in dealing with their own generation than the children of light.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And I tell you, make friends for yourselves by means of dishonest wealth, so that when it fails they may welcome you into the eternal tents.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Whoever is faithful in very little is faithful also in much, and whoever is dishonest in very little is dishonest also in much.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So if you have not been faithful with dishonest wealth, who will trust you with the true wealth?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And if you have not been faithful with what belongs to another, who will give you what is your own?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No household slave can serve two masters; for either he will hate the one and love the other, or he will be devoted to the one and despise the other. You cannot serve both God and wealth.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Pharisees, who loved money, were listening to all this, and they sneered at him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “You are the ones who justify yourselves in the sight of people, but God knows your hearts; for what is exalted among people is an abomination in the sight of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: The Law and the Prophets were until John. Since then the good news of the kingdom of God is being proclaimed, and everyone is forcing their way into it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one stroke of a letter of the Law to fall.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Everyone who divorces his wife and marries another commits adultery, and whoever marries a woman divorced from her husband commits adultery.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: There was a rich man who used to dress in purple and fine linen, feasting splendidly every day.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And a poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gate, covered with sores

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: and longing to eat his fill of what fell from the rich man’s table. Instead, even the dogs would come and lick his sores.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In time the poor man died and was carried away by the angels to Abraham’s side. The rich man also died and was buried.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And in Hades, being in torment, he lifted up his eyes and saw Abraham far off and Lazarus at his side.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He called out, ‘Father Abraham, have mercy on me and send Lazarus to dip the tip of his finger in water and cool my tongue, for I am in agony in this flame.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But Abraham said, ‘Child, remember that in your lifetime you received your good things, and Lazarus likewise the bad; but now he is comforted here, and you are in agony.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And besides all this, a great chasm has been fixed between us and you, so that those who want to cross from here to you cannot, nor can anyone cross from there to us.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said, ‘Then I ask you, father, to send him to my father’s house,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: for I have five brothers, so that he may warn them, so that they too do not come to this place of torment.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But Abraham said, ‘They have Moses and the Prophets; let them listen to them.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said, ‘No, father Abraham, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will turn back.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: He said to him, ‘If they do not listen to Moses and the Prophets, they will not be persuaded even if someone rises from the dead.’”

notes.note: The Greek word names the person, often a slave or freedman, who ran an estate and its accounts on the owner's behalf. 'Steward' is the older English rendering, but the word now suggests a flight attendant or a ceremonial official. Most recent translations also use 'manager'.

The bath (liquid) and the cor (dry, verse 7) are Hebrew units of measure. Their exact sizes in this period are uncertain: a bath was perhaps 20 to 40 litres and a cor perhaps 200 to 400 litres. On any reckoning these are large commercial debts, and the reductions are substantial.

The Greek word can mean the manager's master, as in verses 3 and 5, or 'the Lord', meaning Jesus. Most interpreters take it as the master inside the story, who admires the manager's shrewdness without approving of his dishonesty. A minority take it as Luke's report that Jesus commended the manager, which would end the parable at verse 7.

Luke keeps the Aramaic word mamona, an ordinary term for money and property, which older translations carried over as 'mammon'. It is rendered 'wealth' here because 'Mammon' has since come to sound like the name of a demon; in verse 13 it is pictured as a rival master. 'Dishonest' renders 'of unrighteousness', the same phrase used of the manager in verse 8. Whether it means wealth gained dishonestly or wealth as belonging to this unjust age is disputed.

'They' may be the friends made by generous use of wealth, usually understood as the poor who have been helped. It may instead be an indefinite plural, a reverent Jewish way of saying 'God may welcome you'. The wording deliberately echoes the manager's hope in verse 4 of being welcomed into people's homes.

The Greek word ordinarily means a tent, and in the Greek Old Testament it is the word for the tabernacle and the tents of the wilderness. Most translations generalise to 'dwellings' or 'homes'. 'Tents' is kept because the pairing of a tent with permanence is in the Greek. 'Eternal' here carries the Jewish sense of belonging to the age to come.

notes.phrase: everyone is forcing their way into it
notes.note: The verb form can be middle ('forces a way in') or passive ('is forced' or 'is urgently pressed' to enter). Most translations take it as middle, as here, describing people pushing eagerly, or perhaps aggressively, into the kingdom. Some scholars prefer the passive: 'everyone is urged insistently to enter it'. The saying is compressed and its exact force remains disputed.

The Greek word means the chest or lap, or the fold of a garment over it. The picture is probably of reclining next to Abraham as the guest of honour at a banquet, as in John 13:23, though some see a child held close. 'Bosom' is the traditional rendering and several recent translations use 'side'. The plural form in verse 23 has the same sense.

Hades is the Greek name for the realm of the dead, and the Greek Old Testament uses it for the Hebrew Sheol. It is a different word from Gehenna, the place of final punishment, although in this story the rich man is already suffering there. The scene draws on popular Jewish pictures of the afterlife in which the dead await judgment in separate conditions.

'Repent' in modern English centres on feeling sorry. The Greek word carries the prophets' call to return to God, which is a change of direction in mind and conduct. Most translations keep 'repent' as an established term understood to include a changed life.

candidates.reason: Aramaic loanword in Matthew 6:24 and Luke 16; translators split between 'mammon', 'wealth' and 'money', and the choice should match across the two Gospels.
Recurs in Luke 12, 1 Corinthians 4, Titus 1 and 1 Peter 4, where 'steward' and 'manager' compete and the related οἰκονομία needs a matching decision.
Frequent in the Gospels and Paul; whether to render 'serve' or 'be a slave to' affects how slavery language reads across the whole New Testament.
The ἀδικία/ἄδικος family is the negative of the δικαιοσύνη family and varies between 'unrighteousness', 'injustice', 'wrongdoing' and 'dishonesty' in ways that hide the link.
Recurs in the parables of Matthew and Luke and in Paul as 'wise', 'prudent', 'sensible' or 'shrewd', and needs to be kept distinct from σοφός.
